# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death prevention in patients at risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs), however, are associated with acute and long-term complications related to the intravascular leads, including pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, lead fracture, venous occlusion, and—most importantly—systemic infection and endocarditis requiring complex lead extraction [2,3]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these risks by avoiding intravascular and intracardiac hardware entirely [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, evidence, clinical performance, and limitations of the S-ICD.

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator implanted in a lateral pocket over the left mid-axillary line and a single parasternal subcutaneous electrode [4]. The device senses electrical activity through three sensing vectors and delivers an 80-J shock, substantially higher than transvenous systems because of the greater inter-electrode distance and extrathoracic position [5]. Early feasibility work established that an entirely subcutaneous configuration could reliably defibrillate ventricular fibrillation [4]. Because no leads traverse the vasculature, the S-ICD eliminates lead-related vascular trauma and markedly reduces the risk of systemic infection [6].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated high rates of successful conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation and acceptable complication profiles, supporting regulatory approval [5,7]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed durable performance over several years, with appropriate shock efficacy exceeding 98% for discrete episodes [8]. Observational comparisons between S-ICD and TV-ICD recipients suggested comparable rates of overall complications but differing complication types, with fewer lead-related issues in S-ICD patients [9,10].

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized comparison of S-ICD and TV-ICD in patients with a class I or IIa indication and no need for pacing [11]. It demonstrated non-inferiority of the S-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [11]. Long-term follow-up confirmed sustained safety [12]. The UNTOUCHED study specifically examined inappropriate shock rates in a primary-prevention population with low ejection fraction, reporting low inappropriate shock incidence when modern programming with high-rate cutoffs and dual-zone discrimination was applied [13].

## Inappropriate Shocks and Screening

Inappropriate shocks, frequently caused by T-wave oversensing or myopotential interference, were a major early limitation [14,15]. Mandatory preimplant electrocardiographic screening was introduced to identify suitable sensing vectors and reduce oversensing [16]. Up to 7–10% of candidates may fail screening, particularly those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or bundle branch block [17]. Improved sensing algorithms (e.g., SMART Pass filtering) and dual-zone programming have substantially reduced inappropriate therapy in contemporary practice [18,19].

## Special Populations

The S-ICD is particularly attractive for young patients, those with congenital heart disease, prior device infections, limited venous access, or inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as Brugada syndrome and long QT syndrome [20,21]. In patients on hemodialysis, in whom preserving venous access is critical and infection risk is high, the S-ICD offers theoretical advantages [22]. Registries in pediatric and congenital populations have reported favorable outcomes, though body size remains a consideration [23].

## Limitations

The principal limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to provide long-term bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization therapy [24]. Patients with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia amenable to painless ATP termination may be better served by a transvenous device [25]. The S-ICD generator is larger and battery longevity historically shorter than transvenous counterparts, though newer generations have improved [26]. Implantation technique—particularly the intermuscular two-incision approach—influences cosmetic outcomes and complication rates [27].

## Future Directions

The combination of the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker capable of delivering ATP represents a promising modular approach to overcome the pacing limitation; the MODULAR ATP study has reported encouraging early communication and therapy results [28]. Ongoing refinement of sensing algorithms, generator miniaturization, and improved patient selection through enhanced screening are expected to broaden applicability [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that the S-ICD may be economically favorable in selected high-infection-risk groups despite higher upfront device costs [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD has matured into an established alternative to the transvenous ICD for appropriately selected patients who do not require pacing. Robust randomized and registry evidence supports its safety and efficacy in preventing sudden cardiac death while avoiding lead-related vascular complications. As technology converges with leadless pacing solutions, the indications for the S-ICD are likely to expand further.
